clinicalPearls: A hair-shaft disorder in which the shaft is flattened and twisted through one hundred and eighty degrees at irregular intervals along its length, making hair fragile and easily broken
The hair appears spangled or has an uneven sheen because light reflects differently from the twisted segments
Classic early-onset pili torti often presents in fair-haired children with short, broken, brittle hair, and may be isolated or part of a syndrome
A key association is Menkes disease, an X-linked disorder of copper metabolism in which pili torti accompanies neurodegeneration and connective-tissue features, making it a vital paediatric diagnosis
Other associations include Bjornstad syndrome (pili torti with sensorineural deafness), ectodermal dysplasias and Bazex syndrome
Diagnosis rests on light microscopy showing the characteristic flattened one-hundred-and-eighty-degree twists, while trichoscopy shows alternating bright and dark banding
Management is supportive with gentle hair care and avoidance of trauma, and identifying any underlying syndrome is essential, since some acquired forms improve once the trigger resolves
reference.pathophysiology: Pili torti is a structural abnormality in which the hair shaft is flattened and rotated on its own axis, producing recurrent twists that create points of weakness and increased fragility. It may be a primary genetic defect of hair-shaft formation or occur as part of syndromes affecting ectodermal structures or metabolism; in Menkes disease deficient copper-dependent enzyme activity impairs disulphide bonding and keratin cross-linking. Acquired forms can follow inflammation, scarring or drug exposure. The twisting weakens the shaft so that hair breaks readily.
additionalDifferentials: Trichorrhexis nodosa, with nodal fractures but no twisting
Monilethrix, with a regularly beaded shaft
Netherton syndrome, with bamboo hair (trichorrhexis invaginata)
additionalInvestigations: Light microscopy of the hair shaft showing flattened one-hundred-and-eighty-degree twists
Trichoscopy demonstrating alternating bright and dark banding
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin where Menkes disease is suspected in an infant
Audiometry if Bjornstad syndrome with deafness is considered
Assessment for associated ectodermal or neurological features with genetic testing as indicated
redFlags: An infant with pili torti and neurodevelopmental regression suggesting Menkes disease
Associated sensorineural hearing loss pointing to Bjornstad syndrome
Features of an underlying ectodermal or systemic syndrome requiring urgent evaluation
reference.prognosis: Isolated classic pili torti often improves after puberty, but the outlook depends heavily on any associated syndrome; Menkes disease carries a poor neurological prognosis, whereas isolated or acquired forms may resolve when the cause is removed.
pitfalls: Missing Menkes disease in an infant and so delaying diagnosis of a serious metabolic disorder
Overlooking associated deafness or ectodermal features
Confusing pili torti with other hair-shaft defects without confirmatory microscopy
Attributing brittle hair to hair care alone without examining the shaft
management: Identify and treat any underlying syndrome or acquired cause, since management is directed at the associated condition rather than the hair shaft itself
Advise gentle hair care with avoidance of mechanical trauma, heat styling and chemical treatments to minimise breakage of the fragile twisted shafts
Urgently exclude Menkes disease in an affected infant with serum copper and caeruloplasmin, initiating parenteral copper-histidine replacement where confirmed
Arrange audiometry to detect the sensorineural deafness of Bjornstad syndrome
Assess for associated ectodermal dysplasia and neurological features, with targeted genetic testing as indicated
Provide genetic counselling appropriate to the identified inheritance and refer to multidisciplinary paediatric and dermatological services
Reassure that isolated classic pili torti often improves after puberty, while outlook otherwise depends on the associated disorder
